items.content_html:
What the pipeline did, what broke, and what it chose when something broke. Run 39390907505.

The script shipped 554 words over target, after two expand passes

The first draft came in at 2809 words against a 3400-word target. The pipeline sent it back for up to two expand passes. The script that shipped is 3554 words, which is 154 words over target. The first draft was 591 words short. The expand passes closed that gap and then overshot it.

The overshoot matters because the target is the only length control the pipeline has. Whatever the expand passes added is the part nobody chose, and the review cannot say from these facts where those extra words sit.

Thirteen of eighteen roundup citations matched

The roundup pool had 18 citations, and 13 of them matched. The five that did not match are the gap to watch. The facts do not say whether those five were dropped, paraphrased past recognition, or attached to claims the source does not support. They also do not say which stories they belonged to.

All four deep-dive citations matched. The contrast is the finding. The deep dives are the part of the episode with the most sourcing, and they were the part that held. The roundup stories were the part under pressure, and that is where the unmatched citations sit.

Forty-five roundup stories were cut for airtime

The pool is larger than one segment can air. Forty-five stories were dropped by the airtime budget (NEWS_ROUNDUP_COUNT), and the pipeline treats that as the design working. A cut story can come back on a day when it fits better.

The cut count and the citation gap are separate facts. Forty-five stories were removed before they reached the script. Five citations failed to match among the stories that did reach it. The review does not connect the two, because the facts do not connect them.

The ratio of Casey to Riley lines came out at 1.24

The voice ratio, Casey over Riley, is 1.24. Casey has more lines than Riley, but not by a wide margin. The pipeline recorded one AI-tell pattern hit in the script. The facts do not name the pattern, so the review cannot say whether it was caught and fixed or passed through.

Every scheduled run finished on time, but the first run did most of the work

Three runs were scheduled for this date. The primary run started at 1:05 AM Pacific and finished at 1:38 AM Pacific with a success conclusion. Fallback 1 started at 2:05 AM Pacific and also finished successfully at 2:05 AM Pacific. Fallback 2, started at 3:05 AM Pacific, is the run writing this review and has no finish time yet.

Both completed runs were zero minutes late. The primary run took the full script generation and rendering path. The facts do not say what Fallback 1 did in its 2:05 AM Pacific slot, or why it finished the moment it began. The review does not guess.

In the primary run, script generation took 894 seconds, the longest step. Audio rendering took 286 seconds. Deploying to GitHub Pages took 379 seconds, longer than publishing the episode at 113 seconds. The deploy step is the slowest part of the pipeline after script generation, and nothing in the facts explains why.

The episode runs 21.7 minutes and the video is 75.0 MB

The audio is 21.7 minutes long and 19.9 MB. The video is 21.7 minutes long and 75.0 MB. The two runtimes match, which confirms the video and audio carry the same episode. The file sizes differ by a factor of about four because the video carries the picture track. The feed now holds 265 episodes.

The debate question and the forest-products numbers

The episode's question is whether a forest-products sector shifting toward high-value markets, with a 45 million cubic metre harvest target, serves Cariboo communities, and whose numbers residents should trust during that shift. The four deep dives cover mass timber demand, a Conservative harvest promise, retraining for former South Cariboo forestry workers, and a federal and Ontario investment of up to $50 million. All four deep-dive citations matched, so the question rests on sourcing that checked out.

items.content_html:
What the pipeline did, what broke, and what it chose when something broke. Run 39220293431.

The short draft and the expand passes

The first script draft came in at 2850 words against a target of 3400. The pipeline sent it back for up to two expand passes. What shipped was 3673 words, so the expansion overshot the target by 273 words. The episode is longer than the spec asked for, and the audio reflects it: 21.9 minutes of audio, 20.1 MB.

The degradation log lists one failure, in the script step. Kagi Extract returned no page for 4 thin roundup stories. Those stories were still in the script without their source text.

Citations that did not match

Citation alignment was uneven. Of 17 roundup citations, 13 matched. Of 4 deep-dive citations, 1 matched. The deep-dive figure is the weaker one: three of the four long segments went to air with citations that did not check out against their sources.

The four failed Kagi Extract pages are the likely cause for the roundup side, since thin stories give the matcher less to match against. The facts do not establish that link, so treat it as a suspicion until someone checks which citations were the unmatched ones.

Cut stories

The roundup pool had 40 stories cut by the airtime budget. This is by design. The pool is larger than one segment can air, and a cut story can come back on a day when it fits better. The 40 cuts are not 40 missing items from this episode. They are the pool doing what it was built to do.

The tension is that 4 of those roundup stories were thin enough that Kagi returned nothing for them, yet they still made the script. The budget cut 40 stories, and the thinnest sources were the ones that got through.

Quality and tone

The voice split between the two hosts was 0.93 Casey over Riley. The script tripped the AI-tell pattern check once. Both figures are within what the pipeline is meant to accept, and neither needs action today.

The schedule held, with fallbacks

The primary run started at 1:05 AM Pacific and finished at 1:31 AM Pacific. It completed successfully with no lateness. Two fallback runs were scheduled behind it. Fallback 1 started at 2:05 AM Pacific and finished at 2:05 AM Pacific, also successful. Fallback 2, at 3:05 AM Pacific, is the run producing this review and has not finished.

The slowest steps were the script generation at 502 seconds and the Pages deploy at 371 seconds. Audio rendering took 283 seconds. The video render and YouTube upload took 131 seconds.

Spend and output

The run used 61,831 Anthropic input tokens. API calls split across four services: 11 to Claude, 9 to Brave Search, 4 to Kagi Extract, and 4 to Brave Answers. The video is 75.3 MB at a runtime of 21.9 minutes. The RSS feed now carries 264 episodes.

The day's debate

The episode's question was whether credibility and authenticity in arts and culture come from the artists and audiences themselves, or whether sponsors, founders, and institutions can inherit and spend them. The four deep dives covered a music genre turned into a brand asset, a state crackdown on critics, an architecture archive, and an off-grid refrigerator built from fire and salt. Three of the four deep-dive citations failed to match, so the argument rests more on the scripted framing than on the verified sources behind it.

The short draft that the pipeline sent back twice

The first script draft came in at 2694 words against a target of 3400. The pipeline did not ship it. It sent the draft back for expansion, up to two passes, and what shipped was 3423 words. That is 23 words over target, so the expand passes did their job, but the gap is the story: the generator's first attempt ran about 21 percent short and needed the retry loop to reach length.

The voice split held at 0.87, Casey over Riley, and the AI-tell pattern check recorded zero hits. Neither of those numbers was at risk on this run.

Two takes came back short from TTS

Two text-to-speech takes returned shorter than their word counts predicted. Each was retried once. One retry still came back short. For that segment the pipeline kept the longer of the two takes, so no content was dropped from the episode. The audio ran 22.3 minutes at 20.5 MB.

The short-take count is two and the still-short retry count is one. The second number does not mean one segment is missing from the audio. It means one segment is the one where the retry did not produce a full-length take, and the longer take was used in its place. Whether that take is complete is not something the run measured.

The roundup cut 68 stories and the citations did not fully hold

The roundup pool was larger than one segment could air. The airtime budget, set by NEWS_ROUNDUP_COUNT, cut 68 stories. The pipeline treats that as expected: the pool is deliberately oversized, and a cut story can air on a day where it fits better.

The cuts left a visible tension in the citations. Of 18 roundup citations, 14 matched the aired content. Of four deep-dive citations, three matched. So four citations did not align: one in the roundup and one in the deep dive. The facts do not say which citations failed or why, and this review does not guess.

What the deep dives covered

The four deep dives were drawn from the Gulf attacks coverage in the NYT Business feed, a WIRED piece on microplastics reacting with water, a TechCrunch story on Mosqitter's AI-powered mosquito traps, and an NYT Top Stories piece on worlds more habitable than Earth. The episode's debate question asks whether long-term environmental and scientific monitoring should be trusted and acted on before its implications are confirmed, and how such records should be funded, governed, and sustained. Script generation alone consumed 57,310 Anthropic input tokens. The service call counts were brave-search 8, kagi-extract 4, claude 10, and brave-answers 4. items.title: [Cariboo Signals Reviews] Episode Review — Cariboo Signals, October 16, 2026
items.content_html:
What the pipeline did, what broke, and what it chose when something broke. Run 38871365504.

The script came in short and was padded, not the other way round

The first draft of the script ran 3,129 words against a target of 3,400. The pipeline sent it back for up to two expand passes. What shipped was 3,412 words, which clears the target by 12. The padding was done by the same machinery that wrote the first draft, so the number that reached the listener is not evidence that the first draft was complete.

Two things in the quality block are worth reading against that. The AI-tell pattern check found 0 hits in the shipped script. The voice ratio of Casey to Riley came in at 0.84. Neither number says anything about whether the expand passes added substance or only length.

Six stories aired out of order after two repair passes failed to fix it

The roundup order degraded. Six stories still aired after a later block, even after 2 repair passes. The pipeline did not drop them or re-cut the segment. It let them run in the wrong place and logged the degradation. A listener hears a story from the wrong part of the day's sequence, and nothing in the audio signals that.

The same segment is where the citation numbers are weakest for the deep dives. Roundup citations matched 16 of 17. Deep dive citations matched 1 of 4. The roundup count is a strong match. The deep-dive count means three of the four deep dives have a citation the pipeline could not align to its source, which is a larger gap than anything the roundup shows.

The roundup pool is much bigger than the airtime

The pipeline dropped 59 stories from the roundup pool to fit the airtime budget set by NEWS_ROUNDUP_COUNT. That is the design: the pool is meant to exceed what one segment can carry, and a cut story can come back on a day where it fits better. The 59 are not failures. They are the cost of a fixed airtime, and the pipeline will not show which of them a listener would have wanted.

The four deep dives drew on different sources: Global News, Fast Company, Wildfire Today and NYT Business. They covered a parole decision in British Columbia, heat exposure, Los Angeles fire danger, and California's Proposition 45. The debate question the episode was built around asks who bears the cost of protecting people from wildfire and extreme heat, and whether faster housing review and public ownership of warnings and wildlife data make communities safer or mostly favor developers. Only one of the four deep-dive citations matched, so the sourcing behind that question is the thinnest part of the episode.

Three runs, all on time, one still running

The primary run started at 1:05 AM Pacific and finished at 1:30 AM Pacific. It completed with success and was 0 minutes late. Fallback 1 started and finished at 2:05 AM Pacific, also successful, also 0 minutes late. Fallback 2, at 3:05 AM Pacific, is the run writing this review and has not finished. The fallbacks did not fire because the primary failed. They were scheduled, and the primary succeeded.

The slowest step was script generation at 534 seconds, followed by GitHub Pages deployment at 350 seconds and audio rendering at 266 seconds. Checkout took 75 seconds, publishing 90 seconds, and the video render and YouTube upload 132 seconds. Every step concluded successfully.

The output is 20.7 minutes of audio and 71.7 MB of video

The audio runs 20.7 minutes and is 18.9 MB. The video is 71.7 MB and also runs 20.7 minutes. The RSS feed now lists 261 episodes. The script consumed 62,718 Anthropic input tokens across 11 Claude calls. The service breakdown shows 12 Brave search calls and 4 Brave answers calls. The input-token figure is a count of tokens and says nothing about cost.

The 3,412-word script at 20.7 minutes is the number to hold against the 3,400-word target and the 3,129-word first draft. The audio length is what the listener gets. The gap between the first draft and the shipped script is what the pipeline had to do to reach it.

items.content_html:
What the pipeline did, what broke, and what it chose when something broke. Run 38703190050.

The run that didn't need to fall back, and the script that didn't hit its target

The primary run started at 1:05 AM Pacific, finished at 1:35 AM Pacific, and completed with a success conclusion, zero minutes late. Two fallbacks were scheduled behind it. Fallback 1 started and finished at 2:05 AM Pacific, also a success. Fallback 2, at 3:05 AM Pacific, is the run producing this review. The fallbacks were redundancy, not repair: nothing in the primary's record marks it as failed.

The more instructive mismatch is in the script. The first draft came in at 2,246 words against a target of 3,400. The pipeline sent it back for up to two expand passes, and the script that shipped ran 3,085 words. That is still 315 words short of target. The pipeline did not reach its own goal; it stopped at a figure it judged acceptable, and the facts do not record why that figure and not another.

Roundup coverage: 56 stories cut, and a count that doesn't match

The roundup pool held stories the airtime budget could not carry. 56 were dropped. This is by design: the pool is larger than one segment can air, and a cut story can return on a day when it fits the episode better. The 56 are deferred, not discarded.

Citation alignment on the roundup was 12 of 15 matched. Three roundup citations did not align with the script. The deep dives were worse on the same measure: 2 of 3 matched, so one deep-dive citation went unmatched. Those are the only places where the script and its sources diverge in the record, and the facts do not say which claims the unmatched citations supported.

Three deep dives, one debate, and a voice that leans one way

The three deep dives were a legal action by the FSIN against Ottawa over an audit clawback, a survivors' account from Eagle Feather News, and a return of an ancestral tipi cover reported by IndigiNews. The debate question put to the episode was who holds authority to judge Indigenous governments' financial records, cultural objects, and services, and whether sovereignty survives federal funding conditions and clawbacks.

On voice, the ratio of Casey to Riley lines was 0.9. The script contained zero AI-tell pattern hits. Neither figure is a failure, but the 0.9 ratio means the two hosts were close to balanced in line count, which is the number the pipeline is built to hold.

What shipped, and where it went

The audio runs 19.1 minutes and weighs 17.5 MB. The video runs 19.1 minutes at 66.7 MB, the same runtime as the audio. The RSS feed now carries 260 episodes. The generation step consumed 61,810 Anthropic input tokens across 18 Claude calls, alongside 19 brave-search calls and 4 brave-answers calls. Those are token and call counts, not spend, and the facts give no cost figure.

The slowest step was the script generation at 617 seconds, with checkout at 407 seconds and the GitHub Pages deploy at 350 seconds. Audio rendering took 206 seconds, publish 81 seconds, and the video upload 67 seconds. Every step concluded in success. The run had no warnings to report.
